definition: Anarchist means one who wants to eliminate all government.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word anarchist. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know anarchist should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The old dockhand was an anarchist of the quiet kind, certain that people could run their own affairs with no state above them.
A dissenter is far milder than an anarchist — objecting to this policy or that ruler while leaving government itself standing.
A revolutionary stops short of the anarchist: revolutionaries topple a government to build another, while the anarchist would leave the ground bare.

A rebel fights the particular authority over them and may happily crown a new one once it falls. An anarchist opposes rulers as such: not this king or that law, but the existence of government itself. Every anarchist is against the regime; most rebels only want a different one.

A nihilist rejects all values and meaning — morality, truth, purpose — not just the state. An anarchist's target is narrower and political: government must go, but community, cooperation, and ethics can stay. An anarchist may believe deeply in human goodness; a nihilist believes in nothing.

Anarchist means one who wants to eliminate all government.

At the history fair, Priya's display profiled a 1930s anarchist newspaper whose editors wanted no government whatsoever — not fairer taxes or kinder courts, but no taxes and no courts, with bakeries and bridges alike run by the people who used them.
Anarchist is a precise label, not a loose insult: it names someone who would eliminate all government.
A person who merely breaks rules is unruly; a person who wants lighter rules is a reformer; only the person who wants no rulers at all is an anarchist.
Anarchist is a precise political label, not a synonym for troublemaker: it names someone who would eliminate government itself.
A rule-breaker is unruly; a protester wants better rules.
And keep it apart from libertarian (this unit), who would shrink the state, not erase it.

For her history project, Dara profiled a nineteenth-century printer named Ada Kess, whose little shop produced the city's strangest newspaper.

Kess was not campaigning against one corrupt mayor, as Dara first assumed; she was an anarchist, and her editorials argued that the office of mayor itself -- every office, in fact -- should be abolished.
Yet the paper was not bleak.
Kess organized food pantries and neighborhood repair crews, convinced that neighbors, organized freely, needed no one above them.
The distinction mattered to Dara: Kess believed in rules made face to face, in promises kept, in the town itself -- just never in government.
The paper folded after nine years, but its masthead motto survives in the archive: 'No thrones, no offices, no masters -- and no despair.'
